author: Shaquira Speaks
title: Lancaster County shifting goals for road needs as county continues to grow - NewsBreak
text:
By Shaquira Speaks ,
1 hours ago
LANCASTER COUNTY, S.C. ( QUEEN CITY NEWS ) — As Lancaster County grows, Highway 521 will need to as well. But now leaders will need to find another way to fund more than 100 other road and infrastructure projects throughout the county after voters turned down $253 million transportation tax on Tuesday’s ballot.
The majority of the projects are state-maintained, so county officials’ goals have shifted for now.
“We’ve got to sit down and have a good plan A, B, C, and D, and we’ve got some that we’ve already got in place. We do have a grant in for the State Transportation Infrastructure Bank for $43 million. We actually should hear on that by the end of the year. So we still may be able to move on some projects related to 521. If we get the state support,” Lancaster County administrator Dennis Marstall said.
The funds would’ve given the county a dedicated funding system to match to federal funds that would help complete projects over 10 years.
It’s the second time in two years that voters disagreed with increasing the tax. Last year’s ask was for $405 million.
“Because clearly we don’t want to just keep it. We want to get ahead, plan for growth. That really was kind of what we’re looking at. What are some of the future road needs? 521 widening, certainly,” Marstall said.
Marstall says over the last five months, leaders have been working with developers who’ve completed some improvement projects on 512 turn lanes, specifically, but also some of the new commercial retail. We do have some new intersection improvements that have come along with those. So there is some private sector support for some of the road needs that we have, particularly for 521.
The State Department of Employment and Workforce lists Lancaster County as one of the top areas for concentrated growth.
Officials say Lancaster grew faster than Mecklenburg County, with more people moving in than out.
“We have a growing area where we could have up to 10,000 new homes in the southern part of the county towards Great Falls. So there’s a lot of growth areas that we wanted to address and we will, but we just may be on a more delayed plan than what we thought if we had to continue just to work with the state and use the resources that they made available,” Marstall said.
County leaders will talk about their next steps at the beginning of the year during their annual retreat.
Marstall says the no votes won’t stop leaders from making the county as comfortable as possible.
“We try to communicate during the education campaign was our road funding support really is from the state gas tax and from the State Department of Transportation. We do already have some existing funding through the sales tax, just a little bit. And so we’ll play that out over the next two years, finishing projects. And so we still see some road building projects going forward,” Marstall said.
County officials also don’t use property taxes to fund road projects either.
